questions.title: What is the fundamental difference between value types and reference types in Swift?
questions.answer:
Value types such as `struct` and `enum` provide value semantics: independently stored values behave as separate values when copied and mutated. Classes have reference semantics, where multiple variables may refer to the same instance.

Value semantics do not mean every assignment immediately duplicates all underlying memory. Swift's standard collections often use copy-on-write (CoW).

At Principal level, discuss why value semantics simplify state reasoning and reduce unintended shared mutation, but do not automatically make all operations thread-safe.

questions.title: How does copy-on-write work internally in Swift?
questions.answer:
Copy-on-write allows multiple value instances to share underlying storage until a mutation requires independent storage.

Swift arrays, for example, commonly share a reference-counted buffer. Before mutating, the implementation checks whether it uniquely owns the storage. If not, it copies.

```
var first = [1, 2, 3]
var second = first

second.append(4)

print(first)  // [1, 2, 3]
print(second) // [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

Copy-on-write can make copying large collections inexpensive when no mutation follows. A custom CoW type usually uses a private reference-backed storage class and uniqueness checks such as `isKnownUniquelyReferenced`.

questions.title: Explain some Protocol versus any Protocol.
questions.answer:
`some P` denotes an opaque concrete type that conforms to `P`. The implementation determines the underlying type while callers see only the protocol contract.

`any P` is an existential value capable of holding different conforming concrete types.

Opaque types preserve concrete type identity for the compiler, often enabling more optimization and stronger generic relationships. Existentials provide heterogeneous abstraction but can introduce boxing, indirection or restrictions involving associated types.

Use `some` when retaining a particular hidden concrete type is useful. Use `any` when runtime flexibility matters.

questions.title: How do Swift generics differ from Java-style type erasure?
questions.answer:
Swift generics preserve type relationships in the type system and may use specialization to optimize code for concrete types. Java generics generally erase generic arguments at runtime, with exceptions in how some metadata is retained.

Swift can implement generic functions using metadata and witness tables, and the optimizer may specialize concrete invocations.

However, not every Swift generic invocation is specialized. Code generation depends on optimization, resilience and module boundaries.

Principal-level discussion should include binary size versus performance and the impact of cross-module specialization.

questions.title: What are protocol witness tables?
questions.answer:
Protocol witness tables provide runtime mappings from protocol requirements to a conforming type's implementations.

They support operations on generic or existential values without requiring every conforming type to inherit from a common base class.

A protocol witness table is distinct from the virtual method dispatch mechanism commonly used by classes.

Also distinguish protocol requirements from methods declared only in protocol extensions: extension-only methods are generally statically dispatched based on the available type information.

questions.title: Explain static, virtual and dynamic dispatch in Swift.
questions.answer:
Static dispatch resolves the implementation through compile-time knowledge, allowing potential inlining.

Class methods that support overriding may use virtual dispatch. Objective-C-compatible methods marked `dynamic`, or otherwise routed through Objective-C runtime mechanisms, may use message dispatch.

Swift also uses witness-table dispatch for protocol requirements.

A common misconception is that every class method uses dynamic dispatch. Swift optimization, `final`, visibility and resilience can change the implementation strategy.

questions.title: How does ARC work, and why does it not prevent memory leaks?
questions.answer:
Automatic Reference Counting manages the lifetime of reference-counted objects by retaining and releasing references.

When the relevant strong reference count reaches zero, an object can be deinitialized.

ARC does not automatically detect and collect strong reference cycles.

For example, a view controller strongly owns a callback holder, while the holder strongly retains a closure capturing the view controller. Neither object can be released.

Use weak references where ownership is non-owning, and invalidate long-lived callbacks, subscriptions and tasks when appropriate.

questions.title: When should you use weak versus unowned?
questions.answer:
Both avoid strong ownership.

A `weak` reference becomes `nil` when the referenced object is deallocated, and is typically optional.

An `unowned` reference assumes the target remains alive whenever accessed. Violating this assumption causes a runtime failure.

Use `weak` when the other object may disappear independently. Use `unowned` only when you can prove the lifetime relationship.

For asynchronous callbacks and long-lived operations, `weak` is generally safer because execution may outlive the initiating object.

questions.title: What are escaping and non-escaping closures?
Explain Swift's exclusivity of memory access.
questions.answer:
Swift enforces rules that prevent overlapping incompatible accesses to the same memory.

For example, two overlapping `inout` modifications of the same variable violate exclusivity.

Exclusivity helps Swift preserve value semantics and enables optimizations.

It is not equivalent to full thread safety: programs can still require actor isolation or other synchronization to coordinate independent concurrent tasks.

questions.title: What is a property wrapper, and when would you build one?
What is type erasure and why is it useful?
questions.answer:
Type erasure hides a generic concrete type behind a stable abstraction.

This is useful when protocols contain associated types or `Self` requirements that complicate heterogeneous storage.

Examples include `AnySequence`, `AnyHashable` and custom `AnyRepository<Model>` wrappers.

A typical implementation stores closures or an internal box to forward operations to the underlying value.

The cost is additional indirection, potentially more allocations and weaker compile-time knowledge. Do not introduce type erasure when an ordinary generic type is sufficient.

questions.title: What are associated types, and how do they influence protocol design?
questions.answer:
An associated type is a placeholder type determined by a protocol's conforming implementation.

For example, a repository protocol may declare `associatedtype Entity`.

Associated types are useful when the relationship between input and output types matters.

At an architecture level, consider whether consumers should be generic over the protocol, use a primary associated type constraint, or require type erasure.

Overusing associated types can make dependency injection and module interfaces unnecessarily complex.

questions.title: How do resilient modules affect Swift performance and API design?
questions.answer:
Library evolution allows a framework to change implementation details while maintaining binary compatibility.

Resilience can restrict assumptions that clients make about the layout or implementation of public types.

This affects opportunities for inlining and specialization.

Attributes such as `@inlinable` expose implementation bodies for cross-module optimization, but create compatibility obligations.

In an internal application, source compatibility may matter more than ABI compatibility. In a public SDK, both should be explicitly designed.

questions.title: When should you choose struct, class or actor?
questions.answer:
Choose a `struct` for values with independent state and value semantics.

Choose a `class` when shared identity, reference semantics, subclassing or Objective-C interoperability is necessary.

Choose an `actor` when mutable state needs to be shared safely across concurrency domains.

Actors are not simply “better classes.” Actor isolation introduces asynchronous access boundaries and potential reentrancy concerns.

For UI state, main-actor-isolated observable models are often more appropriate than introducing independent background actors.

questions.title: What is the difference between Equatable, Hashable, Identifiable and Comparable?
questions.answer:
`Equatable` establishes equality semantics. `Hashable` supports hash-based collections and requires equal values to hash equally. `Comparable` defines ordering. `Identifiable` provides identity through an `id`.

These concepts must not be conflated.

Two user profiles might be distinct values but represent the same persistent user identity.

Mutable fields participating in hashing must not change while an item is being used as a key in a hash-based collection.

For SwiftUI, stable identity is crucial for correct state retention and diffing.

questions.title: How would you implement a custom collection?
questions.answer:
First determine whether the abstraction requires `Sequence`, `Collection`, `BidirectionalCollection` or `RandomAccessCollection`.

Provide coherent index semantics, `startIndex`, `endIndex` and subscripting, along with required traversal operations.

Do not promise random access unless indexing operations meet its complexity expectations.

For a ring buffer, consider logical versus physical indices and mutation invalidation.

A Principal Engineer should evaluate whether the custom structure provides enough performance or API benefits to justify maintenance complexity.

questions.title: What are Swift's Codable limitations in complex API models?
questions.answer:
`Codable` is excellent for consistent schemas, but external APIs often contain polymorphic payloads, inconsistent field types, version-dependent fields and dynamic keys.

Use custom `init(from:)`, explicit discriminator enums and carefully controlled lossy parsing where appropriate.

Separate transport DTOs from domain models so inconsistent backend representations do not contaminate business logic.

Avoid broadly ignoring decoding errors, which can silently convert serious contract regressions into corrupted application state.

questions.title: How do throws, Result and typed throws differ?
questions.answer:
`throws` propagates errors through Swift's error-handling control flow. `Result<Success, Failure>` represents an operation's success or failure as a value.

Typed throws, written as `throws(SpecificError)`, allow an API to specify its error type.

Use `Result` when failures must be stored, composed or passed around explicitly. Use throwing functions for natural synchronous or asynchronous control flow.

For a public API, consider error taxonomy, recovery options and compatibility as carefully as the success type.

questions.title: How does Swift bridge to Objective-C?
questions.answer:
Swift interoperates with Objective-C through supported Objective-C-compatible types, `NSObject` inheritance, exposed declarations and bridging mechanisms.

Foundation types such as `NSString`, `NSArray` and `NSDictionary` have bridging relationships with Swift equivalents.

Not all Swift features are representable in Objective-C. Generic Swift APIs, associated types and pure Swift value types may require adapter layers.

A practical modernization approach is to preserve a small Objective-C-facing façade while moving implementation details into Swift modules.

questions.title: What are result builders and how does SwiftUI use them?
questions.answer:
Result builders transform declarative statement syntax into calls that construct structured results.

SwiftUI uses `@ViewBuilder` to combine conditional and sequential view declarations into concrete view composition types.

Result builders do not make arbitrary control flow free or erase all type constraints.

For custom DSLs, they can improve readability, but complex builders often produce difficult diagnostics and opaque abstractions. Prefer straightforward APIs when ordinary functions and types express the problem clearly.

questions.title: How would you design a public Swift SDK?
questions.answer:
Start with the SDK's consumer contract: supported platforms, API stability, error behaviour, threading, privacy and versioning.

Use intentional access control and avoid exposing internal implementation types.

Define clear ownership and cancellation semantics for asynchronous APIs.

Test backward compatibility, binary size, resource usage and failure scenarios. Maintain semantic versioning and migration documentation.

A production-quality SDK also needs telemetry boundaries, security review, reproducible releases and a consumer-facing sample application.

questions.title: What are Swift macros, and when should you avoid them?
questions.answer:
Macros generate Swift code at compile time and can reduce repetitive declarations or provide domain-specific transformations.

They can improve consistency, but they also introduce generated code, build-tool dependencies and debugging complexity.

Use them when the generated contract is understandable and stable.

Avoid macros for logic that is easier to express through generics, protocol extensions or ordinary functions.

At Principal level, assess compile-time cost, developer tooling, testability and maintenance ownership before adoption.

questions.title: What causes retain cycles involving Combine subscriptions or asynchronous tasks?
questions.answer:
A cycle can occur when an object owns a subscription, the subscription owns a closure and the closure strongly captures the object.

Likewise, an object may store a task whose operation strongly captures that object. Even without a permanent cycle, a long-running task can unexpectedly extend the object's lifetime.

Use appropriately scoped cancellation and avoid indefinite work tied to UI objects.

Weak capture is not a universal fix; it must be combined with explicit ownership and lifecycle design.

questions.title: What does a Principal Engineer need to understand about Swift performance?
questions.answer:
Swift performance is affected by algorithmic complexity, allocations, ARC traffic, dispatch, generic specialization, memory locality, bridging and concurrency scheduling.

Value types are not automatically faster than reference types, and protocol-based designs are not inherently slow.

Measure with production-like workloads and Instruments before choosing optimization strategies.

A Principal Engineer should be able to explain whether the bottleneck arises from architecture, I/O, algorithmic complexity, synchronization or code-generation overhead.

questions.title: What problem does Swift structured concurrency solve?
questions.answer:
Structured concurrency ties the lifetime of child tasks to an enclosing operation.

It improves error propagation, cancellation management and reasoning about asynchronous workflows.

`async let` is suitable for a fixed number of concurrent operations; task groups support dynamic collections of child tasks.

Structured concurrency does not eliminate the need for timeouts, resource limits or cancellation checks.

questions.title: How does async/await differ from Grand Central Dispatch?
questions.answer:
`async/await` expresses asynchronous control flow using language-level suspension and task semantics.

GCD schedules blocks on dispatch queues and supplies lower-level synchronization and execution primitives.

An `await` does not inherently block a thread while an operation is suspended.

Conversely, writing `async` does not automatically move CPU-intensive work off the main actor.

For modern application architecture, prefer structured concurrency for asynchronous workflows while retaining GCD where it supplies appropriate interoperability or low-level primitives.

questions.title: What is an actor, and does it eliminate all race conditions?
questions.answer:
Actors protect their isolated mutable state from simultaneous unsynchronized access.

They prevent a class of data races, but logical races can still occur.

For example, an actor may verify that a balance is sufficient, suspend while awaiting an external operation, and later deduct money based on stale assumptions.

Correctness may require transaction-like operations, state revalidation or keeping critical transitions within non-suspending actor-isolated code.

questions.title: Explain actor reentrancy with a practical example.
Explain Task, Task.detached and async let.
questions.answer:
`Task {}` creates an unstructured task that normally inherits the surrounding actor context, priority and task-local values.

`Task.detached {}` creates a more independent task without inheriting actor isolation or task-local context by default.

`async let` creates a structured child task scoped to the enclosing operation.

Prefer structured concurrency when possible. Use unstructured tasks for explicitly managed lifetimes, such as user-initiated work, and detached tasks sparingly.

questions.title: How does cancellation work in Swift concurrency?
questions.answer:
Cancellation is cooperative.

Calling `cancel()` marks the task as cancelled; it does not forcibly terminate execution.

Operations should check cancellation with `Task.checkCancellation()` or `Task.isCancelled`, and respond appropriately to cancellation thrown by participating APIs.

For a search screen, cancellation should also prevent outdated results from updating UI state.

A robust design combines cancellation with request identity checks, because lower-level operations or callbacks may still complete.

questions.title: What is Sendable?
questions.answer:
`Sendable` expresses that values can safely cross concurrency isolation boundaries.

Immutable value types composed of Sendable members can often satisfy this requirement.

Mutable reference types typically require isolation or synchronization.

`@unchecked Sendable` is an explicit assertion that the developer has implemented safety guarantees the compiler cannot verify. It should be treated as a significant review responsibility, not a convenient fix for compiler warnings.

questions.title: How does @MainActor relate to the main thread?
questions.answer:
`@MainActor` isolates declarations to the main actor, which is closely associated with main-thread UI execution.

It provides a concurrency-domain guarantee, not a blanket performance optimization.

A method isolated to `MainActor` can still freeze the UI if it performs substantial synchronous work.

Heavy decoding, image transformations and expensive calculations should be moved to a suitable independent execution context.

questions.title: What changed in Swift 6 strict concurrency?
questions.answer:
Swift 6 language mode strengthens compile-time checking around potentially unsafe transfers of mutable state, actor isolation and Sendable requirements.

A migration can uncover issues hidden by callback-based code, global mutable state and legacy libraries.

An effective migration strategy enables diagnostics, groups issues by module, introduces actor isolation at ownership boundaries and verifies behaviour through tests.

Avoid suppressing warnings broadly with unchecked conformances or unsafe annotations.

questions.title: What is approachable concurrency in Swift 6.2?
questions.answer:
Swift 6.2 added opt-in language and build-setting improvements that make actor-isolated, mostly single-threaded code easier to write.

These include an option for default main-actor isolation, changes to how nonisolated asynchronous functions execute under the relevant language feature, and explicit concurrent execution using `@concurrent`.

The key idea is to make intentional concurrency boundaries clearer instead of implicitly offloading work.

Do not assume every existing Swift target uses these settings automatically.
